verifyNote: Written from UK public health and eye health sources (RNIB, NHS, NICE, professional guidance). Figures are approximate and updated regularly — always check against Dr Sheppard's slides and the latest published statistics.

topics.title: Causes of sight loss in the UK
topics.summary: Around 2 million people in the UK live with sight loss that affects their daily lives, and a large share of it is avoidable. The main causes are uncorrected refractive error, cataract, age-related macular degeneration (AMD), glaucoma and diabetic eye disease.
keyPoints: RNIB estimates more than 2 million people in the UK are living with sight loss; numbers are expected to rise as the population ages.
A large proportion (often quoted as around half) of sight loss is thought to be avoidable or treatable.
Main causes: uncorrected refractive error, cataract, AMD, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy.
AMD is the leading cause of sight impairment certification in older adults.
In working-age adults in England and Wales, inherited retinal disease has overtaken diabetic retinopathy as the leading cause of certification (reported in 2014).
Certification (CVI) is done by a consultant ophthalmologist: sight impaired (partially sighted) or severely sight impaired (blind).
Sight loss is linked to falls, depression, loss of independence and reduced employment.
examTraps: Forgetting that uncorrected refractive error and cataract are major (and correctable) causes.
Saying optometrists certify sight impairment — it's done by consultant ophthalmologists.
Quoting old statistics without a source or date.

diagram.description: Horizontal bar chart (illustrative, not exact) of main causes of sight loss in the UK: uncorrected refractive error, cataract, AMD, glaucoma, diabetic eye disease, other. Bars for refractive error and cataract are labelled 'largely correctable'.

goDeeper.heading: Avoidable sight loss
goDeeper.body: Refractive error is corrected with glasses or contact lenses; cataract with surgery; diabetic retinopathy is detected through screening and treated (laser, injections); glaucoma is detected and managed to slow progression; wet AMD can be treated with anti-VEGF injections if caught early. Regular eye examinations are central to preventing avoidable sight loss.

goDeeper.heading: Certification and registration
goDeeper.body: A consultant ophthalmologist completes a Certificate of Vision Impairment (CVI) when criteria are met. This lets the person be registered with their local council as sight impaired or severely sight impaired, unlocking support (e.g. rehabilitation, benefits, concessions). Optometrists can signpost to low vision services and charities such as RNIB.

flashcards.front: Approximate number living with sight loss in the UK
Leading cause of certification in older adults
Two major correctable causes of sight loss

mcq.q: Which cause of sight loss is most easily corrected?

options.text: Uncorrected refractive error
options.feedback: Yes — glasses or contact lenses.

options.text: Advanced dry AMD
options.feedback: There's currently no cure for advanced dry AMD.

options.text: End-stage glaucoma
options.feedback: Lost vision from glaucoma can't be restored.

options.text: Retinitis pigmentosa
options.feedback: An inherited retinal disease, not easily corrected.

mcq.explanation: Uncorrected refractive error is a leading and easily corrected cause, which is why access to eye tests matters.

topics.askClaude: Summarise the main causes of sight loss in the UK and which are avoidable, then quiz me — and remind me to check the latest figures in my slides.

topics.title: Health inequalities and access to eye care
topics.summary: Eye health isn't equal across society. People in deprived areas, some ethnic groups, people with learning disabilities, care home residents and those facing language or mobility barriers are more likely to have undetected eye disease and less likely to get eye tests.
keyPoints: Deprivation is linked to lower uptake of eye tests and later presentation of conditions like glaucoma.
People with learning disabilities are much more likely to have serious sight problems (often quoted as around 10 times more likely) and often go undiagnosed.
Higher risk groups: Black African and Caribbean people (glaucoma); South Asian people (diabetes and its eye complications).
Barriers: perceived cost of glasses, low awareness of the need for eye tests, mobility, language, fear, and practice accessibility.

NHS sight tests in England are free for many groups, e.g. under 16s, 16–18s in full-time education, over 60s, people with diabetes or glaucoma, and people aged 40+ with a parent/sibling/child with glaucoma, plus those on certain benefits.
Domiciliary (home) eye tests are available for people who can't get to a practice unaccompanied.
The 'inverse care law': those who need care most often get the least.
examTraps: Assuming everyone knows eye tests are free for them.
Forgetting reasonable adjustments (time, communication aids, easy-read materials).
Treating inequality as only about money.

diagram.description: Patient on one side and an optometry practice on the other, with barriers in between drawn as hurdles: cost worries, awareness, mobility/transport, language, fear, disability access. Bridges over each hurdle: free NHS tests, health promotion, domiciliary care, interpreters, reasonable adjustments.

goDeeper.heading: Reasonable adjustments
goDeeper.body: Under the Equality Act 2010, services must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. In practice: longer appointments, quieter times, easy-read information, objective tests when subjective ones aren't possible, involving carers, and accessible premises. SeeAbility has resources on eye care for people with learning disabilities.

goDeeper.heading: Making Every Contact Count
goDeeper.body: Every visit is a chance to check whether family members are eligible for free tests, whether a patient with diabetes is attending screening, and whether someone needs signposting to support. Small conversations can reduce inequality.

flashcards.back: Those who most need care are least likely to receive it.

flashcards.front: Who gets free NHS sight tests in England? (examples)
flashcards.back: Under 16s, 16–18s in full-time education, over 60s, people with diabetes or glaucoma, 40+ with a first-degree relative with glaucoma, certain benefits.
Eye tests at home for people who can't get to a practice unaccompanied.

mcq.q: A 45-year-old whose mother has glaucoma says she can't afford an eye test. What should you tell her?

options.text: She's likely eligible for a free NHS sight test in England
options.feedback: Yes — 40+ with a first-degree relative with glaucoma.

options.text: Eye tests are only free for children
options.feedback: Many adults are eligible too.

options.text: She doesn't need tests until 60
options.feedback: Her family history increases her risk now.

options.text: Glaucoma isn't hereditary
options.feedback: Family history is a major risk factor.

mcq.explanation: In England, people aged 40+ with a parent, sibling or child with glaucoma qualify for free NHS sight tests.

topics.title: Health promotion in practice
topics.summary: Optometrists see many people who don't see their GP often, so small health conversations can make a real difference: smoking, UV, diet, screen habits, diabetes screening and regular eye tests. Behaviour-change models help you pitch advice to where the patient is.
keyPoints: Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor for AMD (smokers are several times more likely to develop it) and cataract.
Very Brief Advice on smoking (NCSCT): Ask, Advise, Act — takes under a minute.
UV protection (sunglasses meeting standards, hats) helps protect the eyes and eyelid skin.
Diet: a diet rich in leafy greens and fish is often advised for macular health; specific supplements (AREDS2) are for certain AMD stages.
Encourage people with diabetes to attend diabetic eye screening and manage blood sugar, BP and cholesterol.
Models: stages of change (precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance), health belief model, COM-B (capability, opportunity, motivation).
Making Every Contact Count (MECC): use routine contacts for brief, opportunistic health advice.
examTraps: Lecturing a patient who isn't ready to change.
Recommending supplements to everyone without an indication.
Forgetting to record the advice given.

diagram.description: Circular diagram of the stages of change: precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance, with a side arrow for relapse returning to an earlier stage.

goDeeper.heading: Very Brief Advice in the chair
goDeeper.body: Ask: 'Do you smoke?' Advise: 'The best thing you can do for your eyes and your health is to stop — and the most effective way is with support from a stop smoking service.' Act: offer details of the local service or refer if available, and record it. Keep it non-judgemental.

goDeeper.heading: Matching advice to readiness
goDeeper.body: Someone in precontemplation needs information and a nudge to think about it; someone preparing to change needs practical help (services, plans); someone in action needs encouragement. Asking 'How do you feel about…?' tells you where they are.

flashcards.back: Precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action, maintenance (and relapse).

flashcards.front: Main modifiable risk factor for AMD

mcq.q: A smoker with early AMD says she isn't interested in stopping. Best approach?

options.text: Give brief, non-judgemental advice and offer support if she changes her mind
options.feedback: Yes — respect where she is (precontemplation), plant the seed.

options.text: Refuse to continue the eye test
options.feedback: Inappropriate.

options.text: Lecture her about all the risks at length
options.feedback: Unlikely to help at this stage.

options.text: Say nothing about smoking
options.feedback: You'd miss an important opportunity.

mcq.explanation: Very Brief Advice works even with people not ready to quit; it raises awareness and opens the door later.

topics.title: Infection control in optometric practice
topics.summary: Keeping patients and staff from picking up infections in practice: the legal duties, how infection spreads, hand hygiene, and decontaminating equipment and trial lenses. Assessed by a pass/fail Blackboard quiz in week 11.
keyPoints: Duties: the GOS contract (infection control and decontamination), the Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 (employer risk assessment), and the Opticians Act duty of care. GOC outcomes 5.5 and 4.8.
Chain of infection: reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Break any link; hands are the main mode.
Handwashing is the single most effective step: at least 15–20 seconds, six-stage technique, then dry with paper towels.
Alcohol rubs (at least 70% for MRSA) are for clean hands between patients and on domiciliary visits; not for visibly dirty hands, C. difficile or norovirus.
Cleaning removes visible dirt; disinfection reduces microbes; sterilisation destroys them all.
Reused trial lenses: don't let them dry, clean, 10,000 ppm sodium hypochlorite for an hour, rinse, then routine disinfection; keep records and inform the patient.
Universal precautions: the routine should already be good enough for patients known to have HIV, hepatitis or CJD.
examTraps: Saying alcohol rub kills C. difficile or norovirus. It doesn't.
Wiping a tonometer head with alcohol alone: it doesn't remove prions and may fix them to the surface.
Cleaning a Volk lens with alcohol: it dissolves the cement.

goDeeper.heading: Drug storage
goDeeper.body: Keep the drug fridge at 2–8°C with no food or drink, check and reset the max/min thermometer daily, keep it lockable, and keep temperature records for at least a year (or the life of the stock) for audit. Date multidose bottles when opened and prefer single-use drops.

goDeeper.heading: When to wear gloves
goDeeper.body: For invasive procedures, if your hands are badly cracked, or if the patient has an infective condition such as viral conjunctivitis. Not routinely for contact lens fitting. Wash your hands before and after, change gloves between patients, and ask about latex allergy.

flashcards.front: Single most effective way to break the chain of infection

flashcards.back: At least 70% ethyl or isopropyl alcohol.
Cleaning: detergent removes visible dirt. Disinfection: heat or chemicals reduce microbes. Sterilisation: all microbes destroyed.

mcq.q: Which is TRUE about alcohol hand rubs?

options.text: They are effective against MRSA if they contain at least 70% alcohol
options.feedback: Yes.

options.text: They are effective against C. difficile
options.feedback: Not effective against C. difficile spores.

options.text: They are effective against norovirus
options.feedback: Not effective.

options.text: They are not recommended for domiciliary visits
options.feedback: They're especially useful where washing facilities are poor, such as home visits.

options.text: They are useful for cleaning visibly dirty hands
options.feedback: Visibly dirty hands must be washed with soap and water.

options.text: Effective handwashing removes up to 50% of microbes
options.feedback: False: proper washing removes about 99 of every 100.

options.text: Alcohol rub can't replace washing if hands are contaminated with bodily fluids
options.feedback: True.

options.text: Drying is part of effective handwashing
options.feedback: True.

options.text: Hands should be washed with antiseptic before invasive procedures
options.feedback: True: e.g. 4% chlorhexidine.

options.text: It is the most important step in breaking the chain of infection
options.feedback: True.

topics.title: Practitioner health and wellbeing
topics.summary: Your own health affects patient safety. Know the signs of stress, where to get help, when a health condition affects fitness to practise or train, and when to tell the GOC.
keyPoints: GOC outcome 5.6: understand the importance of maintaining your own health. Signed off by the stage 2 portfolio task.
Stress: when demands seem to exceed your resources. In optometry it's linked to long hours, time pressure per exam, physical strain and lack of support.
Optometrists report more psychological distress and anxiety than the general population, and many don't seek help.
Fitness to practise or train: the skills, knowledge, health and character to work safely (GOC). Raise concerns about yourself (standard 11.4 for registrants; standard 10 for students).
Declare a health condition to the GOC only if it currently affects your fitness; include the condition, date of diagnosis and treatment, and show insight.
HEOPS standards: reduced stereopsis isn't a bar; colour deficiency is unlikely to be; field defects may stop you meeting competencies.
Conditions that can affect safe practice: alcohol dependence, drug misuse, mental illness, other medical conditions.
examTraps: Thinking every health condition must be declared. Only one that currently affects fitness to practise or train.
Assuming colour vision deficiency stops you training as an optometrist.

goDeeper.heading: Five ways to wellbeing
goDeeper.body: Connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, and give. The AOP peer support line (0800 870 8401) is open to members and non-members; the College also has wellbeing videos, podcasts and articles. See your GP if stress persists.

flashcards.front: Minimum information in a GOC health declaration
flashcards.back: The nature of the condition, the date of diagnosis, and details of any treatment.

flashcards.front: Who can raise a fitness to practise concern with the GOC?
flashcards.back: Anyone: patients, carers, registrants, employers, the police.
Connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, give.

mcq.q: When must a student optometrist declare a health condition to the GOC?

options.text: When it may currently affect their fitness to train
options.feedback: Yes.

options.text: Whenever they're diagnosed with any condition
options.feedback: Only if it currently affects fitness.

options.text: Only once they qualify
options.feedback: Students are registered and make declarations too.

options.text: Never: health is private
options.feedback: Declaration is required when fitness is affected.
